# Build and toolchain: what vet and gofmt catch

**Level:** 201 · anyone who runs `go vet` in CI and wonders what it reads

**One line:** Four vet analyzers read lines the compiler treats as comments — `buildtag`, `directive`, `stdversion` and `tests` — and `gofmt` rewrites two of those lines; the list of what none of them catch is the longer one, and this page ends with it.

## buildtag: a misplaced or mismatched `//go:build` line

<!-- output:build_vet_buildtag_sh -->
*Verified output of [`build_vet_buildtag_sh.sh`](examples/build_vet_buildtag_sh.sh) — regenerated by `tools/run_examples.py`, never hand-typed.*

```text
$ go vet .   # //go:build after the package clause
# example
# [example]
./pricing_fast.go:3:1: misplaced //go:build comment
exit status 1
$ go vet .   # //go:build inside a block comment
# example
# [example]
./pricing_fast.go:2:1: misplaced //go:build comment
exit status 1
$ go vet .   # the old +build line disagrees
# example
# [example]
./pricing_fast.go:2:1: +build lines do not match //go:build condition
exit status 1
$ go vet .   # a space after //
exit status 0
$ go list -f '{{.GoFiles}}' .
[main.go pricing_fast.go]
$ go vet .   # the good version
exit status 0
$ go list -f '{{.GoFiles}}' .
[main.go]
```
<!-- /output -->

**The warning means** — the `//go:build` line is somewhere the go command will not read it (after the package clause, or inside a `/* */` comment), or an old `// +build` line beneath it says something different, so tools that read one line disagree with tools that read the other ([`buildtag` ↗](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/buildtag)).

**The good version** — the last two commands: the line first, a blank line after it, and `go list` shows the file ignored without the tag:

```go
//go:build fast

package main
```

**When the tool is right, and when it is noise.** Right every time it speaks. The case in the middle is the one to notice: `// go:build fast`, with a space, drew no report, and `go list` shows `pricing_fast.go` compiled into the untagged build — to vet it is an ordinary comment, so there is nothing to check. The analyzer's source has a message for that spelling, but the line never reaches it, because the check is only run on comments containing `//go:build`.

## directive: `//go:debug` where it is not honoured

<!-- output:build_vet_directive_sh -->
*Verified output of [`build_vet_directive_sh.sh`](examples/build_vet_directive_sh.sh) — regenerated by `tools/run_examples.py`, never hand-typed.*

```text
$ go vet .   # //go:debug after the package clause
# example
# [example]
./main.go:3:1: //go:debug directive only valid before package declaration
exit status 1
$ go build -o report .
exit status 0
$ go vet ./orders   # //go:debug in a library package
# example/orders
orders/orders.go:1:1: //go:debug directive only valid in package main or test
exit status 1
$ go vet .   # the good version
exit status 0
```
<!-- /output -->

**The warning means** — a `//go:debug` setting is read only from package `main` (or a test), and only before the package clause ([`directive` ↗](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/directive), [GODEBUG settings ↗](https://go.dev/doc/godebug)). Anywhere else the compiler accepts it as a comment — the `go build` in the transcript exits 0 — and the setting is never applied.

**The good version** — the last command:

```go
//go:debug panicnil=1

package main
```

**When the tool is right, and when it is noise.** Right: a `//go:debug` in a library package is the classic mistake, since the setting belongs to the program, not the package, and the `godebug` directive in `go.mod` is the way to set it for a module. Noise: never, in this chapter's measurements.

## stdversion: an API newer than the `go` line

<!-- output:build_vet_stdversion_sh -->
*Verified output of [`build_vet_stdversion_sh.sh`](examples/build_vet_stdversion_sh.sh) — regenerated by `tools/run_examples.py`, never hand-typed.*

```text
$ cat go.mod
module example

go 1.21
$ go vet .   # slices.Concat is new in Go 1.22
# example
# [example]
./main.go:9:18: slices.Concat requires go1.22 or later (module is go1.21)
exit status 1
$ go build -o report . && ./report
[invoice 1042 3 lines]
exit status 0
$ cat go.mod
module example

go 1.20
$ go vet .   # package slices is new in Go 1.21, but the go line is before 1.21
exit status 0
$ go build -o report . && ./report
[10 20 30]
exit status 0
$ go build -o report .   # range over an int is Go 1.22 language, and the go line is 1.20
# example
./main.go:6:17: cannot range over 3 (untyped int constant): requires go1.22 or later (-lang was set to go1.20; check go.mod)
exit status 1
$ cat go.mod
module example

go 1.22
$ go vet . && go build -o report . && ./report
line 0
line 1
line 2
exit status 0
```
<!-- /output -->

**The warning means** — the module's `go` line says which Go the code promises to build with, and `slices.Concat` did not exist in that Go ([`stdversion` ↗](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/stdversion)). The build succeeded anyway: the compiler enforces the *language* version — the `range 3` under `go 1.20` is refused with `requires go1.22 or later` — but not the standard library's API, because the toolchain in use has the function.

**The good version** — the last command, with `go 1.22` in `go.mod`; or the older call the promised Go had.

**When the tool is right, and when it is noise.** Right whenever the `go` line is a promise to someone — a library's users on an older Go build it, and the failure is theirs. The silence in the middle is the case to know: with `go 1.20` and `slices.Sort`, vet said nothing and the build passed, because the analyzer does not report for modules before Go 1.21, when the `go` line became a minimum rather than a hint ([Go 1.21 release notes ↗](https://go.dev/doc/go1.21)). A module whose `go` line predates 1.21 is checked by nobody.

## tests: malformed Test and Example names

<!-- output:build_vet_tests_sh -->
*Verified output of [`build_vet_tests_sh.sh`](examples/build_vet_tests_sh.sh) — regenerated by `tools/run_examples.py`, never hand-typed.*

```text
$ go vet ./orders
# example/orders
# [example/orders]
orders/orders_test.go:5:6: Testcount has malformed name: first letter after 'Test' must not be lowercase
orders/orders_test.go:7:1: ExampleNoSuch refers to unknown identifier: NoSuch
orders/orders_test.go:9:1: ExampleInvoice_Pay refers to unknown field or method: Invoice.Pay
orders/orders_test.go:11:1: ExampleCount should be niladic
exit status 1
$ go test ./orders
# example/orders
# [example/orders]
orders/orders_test.go:5:6: Testcount has malformed name: first letter after 'Test' must not be lowercase
orders/orders_test.go:7:1: ExampleNoSuch refers to unknown identifier: NoSuch
orders/orders_test.go:9:1: ExampleInvoice_Pay refers to unknown field or method: Invoice.Pay
orders/orders_test.go:11:1: ExampleCount should be niladic
FAIL	example/orders [build failed]
FAIL
exit status 1
$ go vet ./orders && go test ./orders
ok  	example/orders
exit status 0
```
<!-- /output -->

**The warning means** — `Testcount` is not a test, because the letter after `Test` is lowercase, so `go test` would run nothing and report `ok`; `ExampleNoSuch` documents an identifier the package does not have; `ExampleInvoice_Pay` names a method `Invoice` does not have; an example takes no parameters ([`tests` ↗](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/tests)). `go test` runs this analyzer as part of its own vet pass, so the package fails with `[build failed]` before any test runs.

**The good version** — the last command: `TestCount`, examples named for `Count` and `Invoice`, and `// Output:` lines that `go test` checks ([An example test checks its output](../../18_Testing/an_example_test_checks_its_output/README.md)).

**When the tool is right, and when it is noise.** Right every time: a misnamed test is a test that never runs. A wrong signature — `func TestCount(t testing.T)` — is caught earlier still, by the go command while loading the test package, with `wrong signature for TestCount, must be: func TestCount(t *testing.T)`.

## gofmt: the blank line, and the `//go:build` line it adds

<!-- output:build_vet_gofmt_buildtag_sh -->
*Verified output of [`build_vet_gofmt_buildtag_sh.sh`](examples/build_vet_gofmt_buildtag_sh.sh) — regenerated by `tools/run_examples.py`, never hand-typed.*

```text
$ gofmt -d pricing_fast.go   # no blank line after //go:build
diff pricing_fast.go.orig pricing_fast.go
--- pricing_fast.go.orig
+++ pricing_fast.go
@@ -1,4 +1,5 @@
 //go:build fast
+
 package main
 
 func pricing() string { return "fast" }
$ go list -f '{{.GoFiles}} ignored={{.IgnoredGoFiles}}' .
[main.go] ignored=[pricing_fast.go]
$ gofmt -d pricing_fast.go   # only the old +build line
diff pricing_fast.go.orig pricing_fast.go
--- pricing_fast.go.orig
+++ pricing_fast.go
@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@
+//go:build fast
 // +build fast
 
 package main
$ go vet .
exit status 0
$ go list -f '{{.GoFiles}} ignored={{.IgnoredGoFiles}}' .
[main.go] ignored=[pricing_fast.go]
$ gofmt -w pricing_fast.go && gofmt -l . && head -3 pricing_fast.go
//go:build fast
// +build fast
```
<!-- /output -->

**The warning means** — there is none; `gofmt -d` shows what `gofmt -w` would change. It inserts the blank line after `//go:build` that separates the constraint from the package documentation, and above a `// +build` line with no `//go:build` it writes the modern line with the same meaning, as it has since Go 1.17 ([Go 1.17 release notes ↗](https://go.dev/doc/go1.17)).

**The good version** — the file `gofmt -w` leaves: both lines, then a blank line. `go list` showed the constraint honoured before and after, so nothing changed but the text.

**When the tool is right, and when it is noise.** Right, and cheap: CI that fails on `gofmt -l` output catches both cases for free. Nothing about a `// +build`-only file is wrong in Go 1.25 — the constraint holds and vet is silent — but the line is the old syntax, and tools written after 1.17 read only the new one.

## What no tool catches

- **`// go:build fast` with a space** — an ordinary comment; the file is in every build, and the `buildtag` transcript above shows vet silent and `go list` compiling it. Only a reader notices, or a test that fails when the wrong file is compiled in ([`//go:build` chooses which files are compiled](../build_constraints_choose_files/README.md)).
- **A `go` line older than 1.21 in `go.mod`** while the code uses a newer API — `stdversion` is silent, the build passes, and the first user on an older Go finds out (the `stdversion` transcript above).
- **A stale generated file** — hand-edited, or not regenerated after its input changed. It compiles, vet is quiet, and only `go generate ./...` followed by `git diff --exit-code` in CI tells ([`go generate` runs a command you name](../go_generate_runs_a_command/README.md)).
- **An embedded file that is edited after the build** — the binary carries the old bytes; nothing knows the edit was meant to be seen ([`//go:embed` puts files in the binary](../go_embed_puts_files_in_the_binary/README.md)).
- **`-X` on a misspelt name or on a variable with a computed initialiser** — exit status 0 both times, and the program says `dev` ([`-ldflags -X` sets a variable at link time](../ldflags_x_sets_a_variable_at_link_time/README.md)).
- **A release built without `-trimpath`** — every binary of the release names the directory it was built in and differs from a rebuild elsewhere; `go version -m` shows no `-trimpath=true` line, but nothing looks unless a script does ([Builds are reproducible with `-trimpath`](../builds_are_reproducible/README.md)).

[staticcheck ↗](https://staticcheck.dev/) and [golangci-lint ↗](https://golangci-lint.run/) read the `// Code generated … DO NOT EDIT.` header and skip such files, and add checks of their own; neither runs in this library.
